questions.statement: The deadline is next Friday, so we need to ____ the project this week.
questions.context: A workgroup is planning the last days before a project deadline.

options.feedback: Correct! 'Get something done' means to finish a task that someone has to complete.
'Give the project' needs a second verb to name what is handed over, so the meaning would be incomplete.
'Take the project' is not a standard collocation with a work task as its object.
'Put the project' only describes its physical location and says nothing about finishing it.

questions.explanation:
The particle 'done' changes the meaning completely: 'get' alone is incomplete, but 'get something done' is a fixed expression for completing work.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: My little brother refuses to ____ his toys before he goes to sleep.
questions.context: A family describes the daily routine of a child before going to bed.

options.feedback: 'Put off' means to postpone, and a bedtime routine is a habit, not a delayed task.
Correct! 'Put away' means to store something in its proper place, which is what a child does with his toys.
'Put up' means to hang something on a wall or to build a tent.
'Put out' means to extinguish a fire or to place something outside.

questions.explanation:
Particles carry their own lexical meaning. 'Away' signals movement to a storage place, which distinguishes 'put away' from the other three.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Rain is unusual in this dry season, so when the storm started everyone ____.
questions.context: Residents react to a rare storm during a normally dry month.

options.feedback: 'Look after' means to take care of someone or something.
'Look up' means to search for information, usually in a dictionary.
Correct! 'Look out' means to pay attention to a possible danger, which is the natural reaction to an unexpected storm.
'Look into' means to investigate a matter in depth.

questions.explanation:
'Look out for' is a warning expression. The unexpected weather is exactly the situation in which the particle 'out' signals caution.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The teacher asked us to ____ our dictionaries after the vocabulary quiz.
questions.context: A class ends a short written activity and the teacher collects the material.

options.feedback: 'Hand out' means to distribute something to several people.
'Hand over' means to give something to someone who takes charge of it.
'Hand back' means to return something that belongs to the person asking for it.
Correct! 'Hand in' means to submit work to the person who will correct or collect it.

questions.explanation:
'Hand in' is the standard term in British and Honduran schools for submitting a paper. The other three particles describe different directions of giving.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The battery of my phone is low; I need to ____ it before the trip.
questions.context: A traveller checks the state of a mobile phone the night before flying.

options.feedback: Correct! 'Charge up' means to give a device the electricity it needs to work.
'Clean up' means to remove dirt or to tidy a place.
'Sign up' means to register for an activity or a course.
'Set up' means to arrange equipment or to establish something.

questions.explanation:
The verb 'charge' selects 'up' in the sense of completing the supply of energy. The other three verbs belong to cleaning, registration and arrangement.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: I cannot meet you at noon, but I can ____ in the afternoon.
questions.context: A student rearranges the hour of a meeting with a classmate.

options.feedback: 'Take off' means to leave the ground or to remove a piece of clothing.
Correct! 'Put off' means to move an arrangement to a later moment.
'Get over' means to recover from an illness or an unpleasant experience.
'Come across' means to meet somebody by chance or to find something.

questions.explanation:
'Put off' is the postponing verb. The afternoon is a later slot, so the appointment has been delayed rather than cancelled.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Our class will ____ a short English presentation on the environment.
questions.context: A high school English class prepares an activity for the school week.

options.feedback: 'Put off' would delay it, and the intention is to hold it, not to delay it.
'Put out' means to extinguish something or to publish a short notice.
Correct! 'Put on' means to organise and perform a show, a play or a presentation.
'Put up' means to erect something or to display a poster.

questions.explanation:
'Put on' is the verb used for a performance of any length. The particle marks the event as something staged in public.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The children ____ the TV every evening and nobody talks at dinner.
questions.context: A family describes an evening in which a television is switched off during dinner.

options.feedback: 'Turn up' means to increase the volume, so the set would still be on.
'Turn on' would start the set, the opposite of the described situation.
'Turn in' means to hand in work or to go to bed.
Correct! 'Turn off' means to stop a machine from working, which is what a television set is doing.

questions.explanation:
Each particle of 'turn' fixes the direction of the change: 'on' starts the device, 'off' stops it, 'up' raises the volume and 'down' lowers it.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: It took me two hours to ____ that error in my essay.
questions.context: A student checks a written text before submitting an assignment.

options.feedback: Correct! 'Find out' means to discover a fact that was hidden, which is what happened with the mistake.
'Look for' means to search for something that is missing, and the error was not lost.
'Figure out' is close in meaning, but 'find out' is the standard expression for discovering news or a hidden detail.
'Carry out' means to perform a task or a plan.

questions.explanation:
'Find out' and 'look for' differ: 'look for' starts an active search, while 'find out' emphasises the result of getting the information.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Please stop ____ the radio; the baby is trying to sleep.
questions.context: A family member gives an instruction in a quiet house at night.

options.feedback: 'Turn on' would make the noise worse, so it contradicts the request.
Correct! 'Turn off' means to switch a device off, and it is what the radio needs here.
'Turn into' means to transform one thing into another and cannot be used with a radio.
'Turn over' means to rotate something or to give it to another person.

questions.explanation:
The gerund after 'stop' names the action the speaker wants to interrupt. The particle decides whether the action starts or stops the noise.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: We ran out of milk this morning, so Dad went to ____ some.
questions.context: A household runs out of a basic item in the morning and someone goes out to solve it.

options.feedback: 'Pick out' means to choose something from a group or to remove an object from a pile.
'Take over' means to assume control of a job or a responsibility.
Correct! 'Pick up' means to obtain or collect something while passing somewhere, as a shop does.
'Set aside' means to save something for a later purpose.

questions.explanation:
'Pick up' implies an incidental acquisition on the way. 'Pick out' would mean a deliberate selection from several products.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The new manager ____ the responsibility of training new employees.
questions.context: A company describes the duties assigned to a recently hired employee.

options.feedback: 'Take over' means to take control of something from a previous holder, which is not stated here.
'Take up' means to start a hobby or a new activity.
'Take in' means to understand an idea or to absorb someone.
Correct! 'Take on' means to accept a duty or a commitment in addition to one's own work.

questions.explanation:
'Take on' adds a new obligation. 'Take over' would require a predecessor and a transfer of authority, which the sentence does not mention.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The meeting was so boring that Luis ____ yawning.
questions.context: Colleagues describe a colleague's behaviour during a long staff meeting.

options.feedback: Correct! 'Keep on' with a gerund means to continue doing something repeatedly, which matches repeated yawning.
'Take after' means to resemble a relative in character or in appearance.
'Get away' means to escape or to obtain something by a trick.
'Put up with' means to tolerate something unpleasant, and it needs a noun.

questions.explanation:
'Keep on' plus a gerund expresses duration. The other three particles belong to resemblance, escape and tolerance.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Do not ____ on me; I already explained the assignment twice.
questions.context: A student responds defensively to a classmate who has not followed the instructions.

options.feedback: 'Cure' is used for an illness, and no health problem is involved here.
Correct! 'Blame someone for something' means to say that person is responsible for it.
'Save' means to rescue or to keep money, and neither sense applies.
'Count on' means to rely on somebody, which is the opposite of what the speaker wants.

questions.explanation:
The verb 'blame' carries the sense of attributing fault, so the objection is coherent. The other verbs do not fit the argument.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The volunteers worked ____ the night to finish the school repairs.
questions.context: A community group describes a night of volunteer work in a school building.

options.feedback: 'Across' means from one side to the other of a physical space.
'Along' means following the length of a line or a route.
Correct! 'Through' means from the beginning to the end of a period, and the whole night was spent working.
'About' means approximately, and it cannot be followed by an article plus a noun in this structure.

questions.explanation:
'Through' expresses duration from beginning to end. The other three prepositions describe a direction, a route or an approximation.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: She ____ the invitation on the table and left the house quickly.
questions.context: A short narrative describes what a character does before leaving a room.

options.feedback: 'Lay off' means to dismiss workers or to stop doing something temporarily.
'Lay out' means to arrange something carefully over a wide area.
'Lay up' means to store something for future use.
Correct! 'Lay down' means to place something flat on a surface.

questions.explanation:
'Lay down' is the particle combination that means to put something flat. The three others belong to employment, arrangement and storage.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The scheme will ____ next month if no one signs the form.
questions.context: An administrator warns about a registration that has not been completed.

options.feedback: Correct! 'Fall through' means that a plan fails to be completed, which is what a missing signature causes.
'Fall behind' means to lag behind others in work or in a class.
'Fall back' means to retreat or to use an alternative plan.
'Fall over' means to lose balance or to stop a machine by turning it off.

questions.explanation:
'Fall through' describes a failure in the process itself. The other three particles describe falling behind, retreating and losing balance.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: He always ____ jokes when he is nervous before an oral exam.
questions.context: A teacher describes the nervous behaviour of a student before a spoken test.

options.feedback: 'Break jokes' is not a standard combination; 'break' would pair with 'a habit' or 'a promise'.
Correct! 'Crack jokes' is a fixed expression meaning to tell jokes, and it is the verb that takes this particle.
'Crash' refers to a collision or to a sudden failure of a system.
'Burst' describes something that suddenly expands, such as a balloon or into tears.

questions.explanation:
The idiom 'crack jokes' is a lexical unit. Knowing the verb alone is not enough: the particle is fixed by the expression.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Our team worked together to ____ the deadline of May 30th.
questions.context: A project team lists the dates it must respect during the year.

options.feedback: 'Beat' a record or an opponent means to do better than them, and a date is neither a record nor an opponent.
'Read' is not used with a date and means to look at the characters on a page.
Correct! 'Meet a deadline' means to finish the work in time, which is the standard collocation.
'Feed' means to give food to an animal or a person, and it never takes a date.

questions.explanation:
The noun 'deadline' collocates with 'meet'. Substituting a different verb breaks the collocation even if the sentence still has a subject and a verb.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: The engine ____ halfway up the hill and the driver had to walk to the next town.
questions.context: Travellers describe a mechanical failure on a mountain road with no workshop nearby.

options.feedback: 'Break out' means to start suddenly, as a fire or an argument does.
'Break up' means to separate something into parts or to end a relationship.
'Break in' means to enter a building by force.
Correct! 'Break down' means that a machine stops working unexpectedly.

questions.explanation:
'Break down' is the expression for a technical failure. The particle 'down' marks the total and sudden stop of the machine.
---
questions.subject: ingles
